evidence_quotes.quote: Drawing from legislative archives, the Mexican American Legal Defense and Education Fund (MALDEF) archives in Stanford University Libraries (Special Collections), and court records, I examine a turning point in the struggle for potable water in south Texas colonias.

The WCIDs resisted the political threat to their power over water by advancing a legislative change that permitted WCID governing boards to unilaterally exclude “urban property” (colonias) from their districts.
Had the legislature not made this change to include informal settlements, a majority of colonias could not have been excluded from the district.
Initially, the denial was based on the grounds that the applicants did not own land in the district as required by the Texas Water Code.
Eleven tracts did not have domestic water service for 325 houses.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community potable/domestic water service access (and associated sanitation deficits) in low-income Mexican-American rural and periurban subdivisions (colonias) in the Lower Rio Grande Valley of South Texas.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines legal, legislative, regulatory, and water-district governance factors shaping colonias water access. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it specifically analyzes concrete legal and regulatory rules directly governing utility/district service boundaries, eligibility, tenure/documentation, procedural notice, and utility regulatory structure: (1) the 1971 Texas statute (Article 8280-3.2) empowering Water Control and Improvement District (WCID) boards to unilaterally de-annex 'urban property' explicitly amended to capture unplatted/unrecorded colonias subdivisions; (2) Texas Water Code freeholder (landownership) requirements for water-district candidacy and franchise; (3) English-only courthouse/newspaper constructive notice rules for de-annexation hearings; and (4) judicial and statutory classification of WCID regulatory mandates as narrow special-purpose irrigation districts (followed by formal conversion into Irrigation Districts) exempting them from providing treated domestic water service. Plain=yes and Narrow=yes.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical qualitative socio-legal / archival historical case study drawing on primary legislative archives (Texas State Archives Bill File), archival litigation files and correspondence from the Mexican American Legal Defense and Education Fund (MALDEF) Special Collections at Stanford University Libraries (including stipulations of fact, preliminary hearing transcripts, amended complaints, and briefs), court rulings, and personal communication with district personnel.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete exclusion and service-access outcomes, including formal territorial de-annexation of 39 rural and periurban subdivisions (743 acres / 2,950 lots, including 11 tracts with 325 houses lacking domestic water service and other lots where residents could not afford rural water supply company charges) by Hidalgo WCID 2, exclusion of 4 subdivisions by H&C WCID 9, subsequent post-1976 de-annexations of additional colonias through 1980, and foreclosure of treated domestic water supply from regional water districts.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies population and units of analysis (colonias subdivisions/tracts, residents, water districts [Hidalgo WCID 2 and H&C WCID 9], and companion litigation cases in South Texas), legal/regulatory exposures (1971 unilateral de-annexation statute targeting unplatted urban property, freeholder requirements, notice rules, and special-district regulatory classification), exclusion/access outcomes, and qualitative archival socio-legal case study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English (with an accompanying Spanish abstract), which is directly eligible without translation.

population_and_sample: Low-income Mexican-American rural and periurban subdivisions (colonias) and residents in the Lower Rio Grande Valley, South Texas, focusing on subdivisions excluded by Hidalgo County WCID No. 2 (39 subdivisions, 743 acres / 2,950 lots, including 325 unserved houses across 11 tracts) and Hidalgo & Cameron Counties WCID No. 9 (4 subdivisions), and the companion federal lawsuits (14 plaintiffs across 9 excluded subdivisions in Jimenez and 2 board candidates in Fonseca, 1971-1976). Units of analysis: settlement/subdivision (colonia), water district (WCID), and judicial litigation proceedings.
exposure: 1971 Texas statutory amendment (Article 8280-3.2) authorizing Water Control and Improvement District (WCID) boards to unilaterally exclude/de-annex platted and unplatted 'urban property' subdivisions, Texas Water Code freeholder (landownership) candidacy/franchise rules, constructive English-only de-annexation notice procedures, and judicial/regulatory classification of WCIDs as narrow special-purpose irrigation districts (Jimenez v. Hidalgo WCID 2 and Fonseca v. Hidalgo WCID 2).
outcome: Territorial exclusion (de-annexation) of colonias subdivisions from WCID service/electoral boundaries (39 subdivisions / 2,950 lots in Hidalgo WCID 2, 4 subdivisions in H&C WCID 9, and widespread de-annexations by 1980), disenfranchisement in district governance, and denial/non-provision of treated domestic water supply by WCIDs (leaving 325 houses across 11 excluded tracts with no domestic water service and others facing unaffordable rural water supply company rates or reliance on shallow wells and cisterns).
rationale: This full-text peer-reviewed empirical socio-legal / critical legal geography study meets all inclusion criteria (c1-c6). Using primary legislative archives, MALDEF Special Collections litigation archives (stipulations of fact, hearing transcripts, briefs, correspondence), court records, and district personnel communication, Jepson (2012) examines how concrete statutory and regulatory rules—specifically Texas's 1971 unilateral de-annexation statute expanded to cover unplatted colonias subdivisions, freeholder/landownership requirements under the Texas Water Code, constructive notice rules, and special-purpose district regulatory classification—directly governed territorial exclusion of colonias from Water Control and Improvement Districts and foreclosed treated domestic water provision. Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies with clear archival data and rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access and exclusion are explicitly eligible for inclusion in the systematic review.
